prompt: What is the difference between expiration and eviction?

options.text: Expiration removes entries past their TTL; eviction removes entries to make room when the cache is full
They are two names for the same thing
Expiration happens only when the cache is full
Eviction removes entries that are wrong; expiration removes popular ones

explanation: Expiration is about freshness and happens on a timer; eviction is about capacity and happens under memory pressure. (b) conflates them. (c) describes eviction, not expiration. (d) Neither mechanism knows whether an entry is wrong, and no sane policy targets popular entries.

prompt: Under LRU, which key is evicted when E is inserted?
scenario: An LRU cache holds 3 entries. It receives the requests A, B, C, B, A, then E.

options.text: A
B
C
E is rejected

explanation: After A, B, C, B, A the recency order (oldest first) is C, B, A, so C is least recently used. (a) A was just used. (b) B was used after C. (d) LRU always admits the new entry and evicts the victim.

prompt: What most likely caused the morning's low hit ratio?
scenario: A product cache uses plain LRU and runs at 97% hits all day. Every night at 02:00 a reconciliation job reads every one of 4 million products once through the same cache. Each morning the hit ratio starts near 40% and takes an hour to recover.

options.text: The job's one-off reads became the most recent entries and evicted the hot set (cache pollution)
The TTLs are too long
The cache node restarts every night
LRU evicts the most recently used keys first

explanation: A scan makes millions of keys 'recent', pushing out the hot ones; morning traffic then misses until they reload. Fix it by routing the job around the cache or using a scan-resistant policy such as LFU. (b) Long TTLs would raise the hit ratio, not lower it. (c) Nothing suggests a restart, and the timing matches the job. (d) LRU evicts the least recently used.

prompt: Why does an O(1) LRU cache use a doubly linked list rather than a singly linked list?

options.text: To unlink a node in O(1), you need a pointer to its previous node
Doubly linked lists use less memory
So the list can be sorted by key
Singly linked lists can't hold more than one entry

explanation: Moving a hit entry to the front means unlinking it from the middle, which needs its predecessor; a singly linked list would need an O(n) walk. (b) They use more memory: one extra pointer per node. (c) LRU orders by recency, not key. (d) is simply false.

prompt: In the hash map + doubly linked list LRU, which operations are O(1)? (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: Looking up a key
Moving a hit entry to the most-recent end
Finding and removing the least recently used entry
Listing all keys in recency order

explanation: (a) is a hash map lookup. (b) is a constant number of pointer changes. (c) The victim is always the node next to the tail sentinel. (d) is O(n) because it must visit every node.

prompt: Why does a shared in-process LRU cache become a bottleneck on a many-core server?

options.text: Every get reorders the list, so every access, even a read, needs exclusive access to shared state
Hash maps can't be read concurrently by design
LRU caches must write to disk on every hit
The capacity is divided by the number of cores

explanation: Reads mutate recency order, so they contend on a lock; libraries shard the cache or batch access updates. (b) Concurrent hash map reads are routine. (c) In-memory caches don't touch disk on hits. (d) Capacity doesn't depend on core count.

prompt: What is the problem with this LFU cache?
scenario: A video site's cache uses pure LFU with no decay. Last month's viral video, with 40 million hits, is still cached. Today's trending videos, each with a few thousand hits, keep getting evicted and reloaded.

options.text: Without decay, old counts never fade, so stale favourites crowd out what's popular now
LFU always evicts the most popular entry
The cache is using LRU by mistake
The viral video's TTL is too short

explanation: Pure LFU remembers all history; decaying counts (as Redis's LFU mode does) lets past popularity fade. (b) LFU evicts the least frequently used. (c) Under LRU the old video would have been evicted long ago. (d) A short TTL would have removed the old video, which is the opposite of what's happening.

prompt: Which is a real advantage of FIFO eviction over LRU?

options.text: It never evicts hot keys
It does no bookkeeping on hits, so reads don't contend on shared state
It always achieves a higher hit ratio
It doesn't need a capacity limit

explanation: FIFO only acts on insert and evict, so hits are cheap and concurrent. (a) It can evict hot keys just because they're old. (c) Plain FIFO usually hits less than LRU; only some FIFO-based variants compete. (d) Every eviction policy exists because of a capacity limit.

scenario: A team starts a fresh Redis instance, sets `maxmemory 4gb`, and uses it as a cache with a 1-hour TTL on every key. Under peak load, writes start failing with out-of-memory errors while reads keep working.

options.text: The default maxmemory-policy is noeviction, so Redis rejects writes once memory is full instead of evicting
TTLs disable eviction
Redis can't store more than 4 GB
The keys are too large to evict

explanation: With noeviction, hitting maxmemory makes memory-needing writes fail. More than 4 GB was written within one TTL period, so expiry alone couldn't keep up. Set allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu. (b) TTLs make keys eligible for volatile-* policies; they don't disable eviction. (c) 4 GB is the configured limit, not a Redis maximum. (d) Key size doesn't block eviction.

prompt: Which policy lets the cache entries be evicted while protecting the sessions?
scenario: One Redis instance holds user sessions, which must never be evicted, and cached page fragments, which can be. Memory is nearly full.

options.text: allkeys-lru, with no TTLs anywhere
volatile-lru, with TTLs set on page fragments and no TTL on sessions
noeviction
allkeys-random

explanation: volatile-* policies only evict keys that have a TTL, so fragments with TTLs are candidates and sessions without TTLs aren't. Separate instances would be cleaner still. (a) and (d) could evict sessions. (c) would make writes fail instead of evicting fragments.

options.text: It keeps a full doubly linked list across all keys
It samples a few keys (maxmemory-samples, default 5) and evicts the one idle longest, keeping a pool of candidates between rounds
It evicts keys in alphabetical order
It evicts the largest keys first

explanation: Sampling with a per-key access stamp avoids per-key list pointers. (a) is exactly what Redis avoids to save memory. (c) and (d) aren't Redis policies.
